I am planning to construct a residential complex with more than twelve houses. I plan to give them on rent to various persons. I have given contract to a contractor to build the complex for me. Should the contractor charge service tax from me? The service of residential complex is not taxable if the residential complex is intended for personal use as residence. As per Explanation ( a) to section 65(91a ), ‘personal use’ includes permitting the complex for use as residence by another person on rent or without consideration. Thus, in your case, the service is not taxable.

The question will arise if you after some time, decide to sell the flats instead of giving these on rent. In such case, the service tax cannot be levied, as what is important is the nature of service at the time of providing service. Subsequent events cannot change the nature of service provided, particularly when the words used are ‘intended for personal use’ and not ‘used for personal residence’.

When construction of residential complex services can be treated as ‘export of service’ for exemption of service tax ?

In case of construction of residential complex services, the service will be ‘export of service’ only if - (a) the immovable property is situated abroad, (b) the service is delivered outside India and used in business or for any other purpose outside India and (c) payment for such service is received in convertible, i.e., free foreign exchange.

What is the value for purpose of calculation of service tax?

Service tax is payable on gross amount charged for service provided or to be provided.

Often contract for construction of complex is a compo-site contract, i.e., inclusive of material cost. In such cases, instead of identifying value of taxable services in a composite contract, tax on service of construction of residential complex can be paid on 33 per cent of gross amount charged. This would be so if (a) the gross amount charged includes value of goods and materials supplied or provided or used by provider of the construction service for providing such service and (b) Cenvat credit of inputs and capital goods is not availed. This simple method is not available in case of only completion and finishing services (Notification No. 18/2005-ST dated June 7, 2005).

Is there a simple method to pay service tax?

A service provider providing taxable service of construction of residential complex can opt to pay service tax on 33 per cent of gross amount charged. The gross amount should include value of goods and materials supplied or provided or used. However, he can avail this concession only if - (a) He does not avail Cenvat of duty paid on inputs and capital goods (He can avail Cenvat of input services) and (b) He does not avail benefit of Notification No. 12/2003-ST dated June 20, 2003 and Notification No. 18/2005-ST dated June 7, 2005.

This simple method is not available in case the service provider provides only completion and finishing services (as in such cases, material content will be much less).

The partial exemption is available only if the gross amount charged includes value of goods and materials supplied or provided or used by provider of the commercial or industrial construction service for providing such service [Explanation to Notification No. 18/2005-ST]. Thus, if the customer provides some material, its value will have to be added for purpose of payment of service tax.

As per Notification No. 12/2003-ST, no service tax is payable on value of material or goods sold to recipient of service. Thus, if a service provider avails exemption under 15/2004-ST, he cannot avail concessional rate of 33 per cent of gross amount charged to customers.

The service provider can have benefit either under No. 12/2003-ST or No. 15/2004-ST and not both.

After having imposed service tax on industrial and commercial construction a few years back, the Finance Minister has stretched the levy to residential construction also. Introduction

1. The exponential growth of the ‘construction industry’ has surely not gone unnoticed. At least, the Government has an eye on the sector. The biggest award that the Government gives to all growing sectors is taxes - asking for their share in the growth. Also the Government has been smart enough to levy the same in a phased manner so that it goes smoothly without attracting too much burden. After imposing service tax on industrial and commercial construction under the entry ‘construction of industrial or commercial buildings’ few years back, the Finance Minister had stretched the levy to ‘residential constructions’ also. So much for the National Policy of providing a shelter to all and consequent concessions to the industry being given under Direct Tax Laws, the sub-section targets the construction activity for the not so privileged, namely, residential complexes. Nevertheless, the levies have been imposed and it will be better to discuss them rather than complaining.

Construction of complex service

2. This is one of the latest services to be included in the service tax basket. It has been added through a sub-clause (zzzh) of clause (105) of section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 that reads as:

"(105) ‘taxable service’ means any service provided or to be provided,—

( zzzh)to any person, by any other person, in relation to construction of complex,

and the term ‘service provider’ shall be construed accordingly."

The levy has been made under a new sub-clause and has not been made by amending the sub-clause (zzzq) of clause (105) of section 65 dealing with commercial or industrial construction service. Though currently all services are being charged at a common rate of 10 per cent plus a surcharge amounting to 2 per cent, (12 per cent once the Finance Bill gets approved) this may, however, mean that in the long run the Finance Minister may have plans to tax commercial construction and residential construction at different rates.

The charging clause is clear and covers all service providers and all persons receiving the service. Unlike some other services where the service is taxable only if provided to a client or customer, in the case of commercial complex, the service is taxable when it is offered to any other person. This means that even sub-contractors providing services to a contractor or builder will have to collect and deposit service tax and will have to make all the compliances. The main contractor can take CENVAT credit for the same.

2.1 What is construction of a complex? - The term has been defined in clause (30a) of section 65 as—

"30(a) ‘construction of complex’ means—

(a )construction of new residential complex or a part thereof; or

(c)repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services in relation to, residential complex."

In all the above 3 sub-clauses (a), (b) and (c ), there is a common phrase which also needs proper definition for clear understanding.

2.2 What is a residential complex?

"(91a) ‘residential complex’ means any complex comprising of—

YOUR QUERIES ON SERVICE TAX

RAJESH DHAWAN*

Whether charges collected by Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) towards marketing fee fall under ‘Technical inspection and certification services’ ?

Yes. In the case of Grasim Industries Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 21 STT 128 (Chennai - CESTAT), the Tribunal held that charges collected by BIS towards marketing fee are part and parcel of the cost of the services rendered by the agency and, therefore, marketing fee charged by BIS is includible in the value of taxable service and subject to service tax.

Whether lease rental falls under ‘Airport services’ ?

No. The Government in its Circular No. 80/10/2004-ST, dated 17-9-2004 has clarified that in case a part of airport/civil enclave premises is rented/leased out, the rental/lease charges would not be subjected to service tax, as the activity of letting out premises does not amount to rendering a service under the category of ‘Airport services’. With effect from 1-6-2007, service tax has been levied on renting of immovable property for commercial purpose and same falls under ‘Renting of immovable property services’.

Whether advertising service falls under ‘Business exhibition services’ ?

No. The Government in its Circular No. 80/10/2004-ST, dated 17-9-2004 has clarified that while services rendered in relation to a circular, label, documents, hoardings or any other audio visual representation of a product or service fall under ‘Advertisement services’, the services relating to actual exhibition or display of product or services would fall under the category of ‘Business exhibition services’.

Whether construction of road in commercial complex falls under ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’ ?

Yes. The Government in Instruction No. vide TRU’s letter F.No. B1/6/2005-TRU, dated 27-7-2005 has clarified that if the contract for construction of commercial complex is a single contract and the construction of road is not recognised as a separate activity as per the contract, then service tax would be leviable on the gross amount charged for construction including the value of construction of roads.

Whether services provided by IRCTC in trains fall under ‘Outdoor caterer services’ ?

Yes. In the Shatabadi/Rajdhani trains, the IRCTC-licensed private contractors (known as sub-licencees) provide catering services to passangers on boarding the trains and the private contractor pays service tax under the outdoor catering service classifiable under section 65(105)(zzt ) of the Finance Act, 1994 for the catering services provided. The Government in its letter, F. No. 332/38/2006-TRU, dated 1-8-2006, has clarified that "in view of the definition of ‘outdoor catering service’ under section 65(105)( zzt), outdoor caterer under section 65(76a) and caterer under section 65(24) and, the service provided by IRCTC appear to be classifiable under ‘Outdoor catering services’."

In the case of SAJ Flight Services (P.) Ltd. v. Superintendent of Central Excise [2006] 3 STT 165 (Ker.), the Court held that supply of foods and beverages to aircrafts for service to the passengers on board will attract service tax under ‘Catering services’.

Whether service provided by club or trade association to its member falls under ‘Services by club or association’ ?

Yes. The Board in the Instruction No. 137/50/2008-CX.4, dated 5-3-2008 has clarified that the services provided by club to its own members, or to the guest of the members are subject to service tax under the ‘Club or association services’ and the plea that they are providing the service to their own member, is not sustainable.

Whether repair, renovation, etc., of old residential complex falls under ‘Construction of residential complex services’ ?

Yes. The definition of ‘Construction of complex’ includes repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services in relation to, residential complex. The Government in its departmental instructions vide TRU’s letter F. With the passing of the Finance Act, 2005, certain new services are brought into the tax net vide, Notification No. 15/2005-ST, dated June 7, 2005 and the construction service relating to construction of complex also came into the tax net with effect from June 16, 2005. Some of the important definitions and their implications and the general and specific exemptions available through various notifications are analytically discussed here. Who will be liable to pay service tax under this service and what are the exemptions and options available to the service provider are also discussed.

Introduction

1. The construction activity was brought under the service tax net with effect from September 10, 2004. But it was limited to commercial construction, i.e., the construction of building primarily used for commercial purpose. However, in the recent Finance Bill, i.e., Finance Bill, 2005, the scope of the construction activity was proposed to be widened to include construction of building to be used for residential purpose. Since the said Finance Bill, 2005 has now become the Finance Act, 2005 and the new services in the said Act are brought into tax net from June 16, 2005 vide Notification No. 15/2005-ST, dated June 7, 2005, the construction service relating to construction of complex has also come into tax net from June 16, 2005. Some important definitions such as ‘construction of complex’, ‘residential complex’, ‘residential unit’, etc., in relation to this category are discussed in the succeeding paragraphs.

Scope of new levy on ‘construction of complex’

2. Clause (30a) of section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 defines the term ‘construction of complex’ as,—

"(a )construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof; or

(b )completion and finishing services in relation to residential complex such as glazing, plastering, painting, floor and wall tiling, wall covering and papering, wood and metal joinery and carpentry, fencing and railing, construction of swimming pools, acoustic applications or fittings and other similar services; or

(c )repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services in relation to, residential complex;"

This definition gives the scope of the category of service, i.e. , this definition gives the type of services (which are actually related to construction activity) which are taxable if provided in relation to construction of building which is primarily used for residential purpose.

According to the above definition, ‘construction of complex’ may be divided into three categories of services, they are :

(i)Construction of building or buildings itself which is used for residential purpose.

(ii)Allied services in relation to completion or finishing of complex such as glazing, plastering, painting, floor and wall tiling, wall covering and papering, wood and metal joinery and carpentry, fencing and railing, construction of swimming pools, acoustic applications or fittings and other similar services.

(iii)Repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of residential complex.

It, therefore, follows that not only construction activity of complex is taxable but also the allied services of construction as stated above are also taxable under this category. Even renovation, restoration and similar services in relation to the complex are also taxable. It can be concluded that the construction service itself and major services allied to it are now taxable if provided in relation to residential complex.

The author has explained the scope and ambit of ‘Construction of Complex’ service, which is one of the nine new services that have been proposed to be brought to service tax levy in the Finance Bill, 2005. The author has analysed the provisions by comparing them with the provisions already in force in respect of ‘Construction Service’, and has suggested that, in the interest of the common man, the tax incidence on this service should be kept minimal.

Introduction

1. The concluding paragraph of the Hon’ble Finance Minister’s speech on Union Budget 2005-06, reads as follows:

One of India’s proudest sons, Dr. Amartya Sen, argues in his book ‘Development as freedom’ that development is a process of expanding the real freedoms that people enjoy. He says, "Growth of GNP or of individual incomes can, of course, be very important as means to expanding the freedoms enjoyed by the members of the society. But freedoms depend also on other determinants, such as social and economic arrangements (for example, facilities for education and health care) as well as political and civil rights." The UPA Government accepts this ethical dimension to the discussion of economic issues, and in this Budget, I have attempted to reflect that dimension. More or less the same idea was articulated two thousand years ago by Saint Tiruvalluvar who said:

"Pini Inmai Selvam Vilaivu Inbam Emam

Ani Enba Nattirkku Iv Iyndhu"

(Health, wealth, produce, the happiness, that is the result and security.

These five, the learned say, are the ornaments of polity)

In this backdrop, let us consider the fate of a middle-income and even an upper-middle income citizen. He has a dream to have a house of his own. He saves for a long period and then buys a house with the help of probably a housing finance institution. He pays stamp duty, registration charges, real estate agent’s commission, society formation charges, and consultant’ fees etc., besides the price paid to the builder. Now he will have to bear the brunt of service tax proposed to be levied in the budget. If a news item in Times of India is any indication, the prices of the residential houses will go up by minimum 3 per cent. The million dollar question begging an answer is whether service tax on housing complexes is justified?

The proposal

2. Before answering the above question, let us understand this new proposal. The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 had included services provided by a commercial concern in relation to construction, repairs, alteration or restoration of such buildings, civil structures or part thereof which are used, occupied or engaged for the purposes of commerce and industry. There was hardly any opposition to this proposal as this covered only commercial and industrial structure. However, the proposal contained in the Budget 2005-06 intends to cover even residential complexes. Clause (30a) of section 65 is proposed to be replaced by the following clause:

‘Construction of complex’ means—

(a)construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof; or

(b)completion and finishing services in relation to residential complex such as glazing, plastering, painting, floor and wall tiling, wall covering and wall papering, wood and metal joinery and carpentry, fencing and railing, construction of swimming pools, acoustic applications or fittings and other similar services; or

(c)repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services in relation to, residential complex.

Thus, it can be seen that the net is very wide and almost everything in relation to upkeep and repair of a residential premises or building is sought to be covered.

What is a residential complex

3. The new proposed clause (91a) defines a ‘residential complex’ to mean any complex comprising of—

‘(i)a building or buildings, having more than twelve residential units;

(ii)a common area; and

(iii)any one or more of facilities or services such as park, lift, parking space, community hall, common water supply or effluent treatment system, located within a premises and the layout of such premises is approved by an authority under any law for the time being in force, but does not include a complex which is constructed by a person directly engaging any other person for designing or planning of the layout, and the construction of such complex is intended for personal use as residence by such person.

Explanation —For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that for the purposes of this clause,—

(a)"personal use" includes permitting the complex for use as residence by another person on rent or without consideration;

In case of an existing residential complex, which already has more than 12 residential units, service tax is required to be levied on all further construction related activity. The above conclusions draw their support from sub-clause (a) that reads as ‘Construction of new residential complex or a part thereof’. Whether painters, plumbers and carpenters, etc., can be covered under the levy

7. Though it seems a bit odd, the new levy shall cover the services of petty workers like painters, plumbers and carpenters, etc., if they are provided in relation to a residential complex. However, they may not be advised to run to the service tax department to get them registered as thankfully a basic exemption limit of Rs. 4 lakhs has been introduced this year. In case you live in a residential complex do not get surprised if at this Diwali your city’s famous painter adds additional service tax with the whitewash bill.

Conclusion

8. To conclude, the scope of each and every service has been increased year-by-year and what is not covered this year will surely be covered in the years to come. The levy of service tax has been expanded this year by adding 9 more services and also by expanding the coverage of 12 existing services. Much larger revenue can be added to the exchequer only by ensuring proper execution of the law. The Finance Ministry has this year not shown favour with the long-term national objective of providing shelter to all by the above levy. The tax is going make the homes for middle and upper middle class people still costlier while leaving the other sections who could afford the tax better unaffected.

4.2 Common area and facilities with approved plan - Such a residential complex must have a common area and certain facilities, such as park, lift, parking space, etc. so that the complex can be conveniently used by the occupants. Moreover, the layout of such a premises must be approved by the competent authority. Such a complex would not include a complex which is meant for personal use of the owner. In other words, such complexes are used for commercial or industrial purposes and not for personal purposes.

4.3 Provision relating to ‘residential complex’ to be read with the provision of ‘commercial or industrial construction service’ - In this connection, it is pertinent to point out that the expression ‘residential complex’ is to be read with the provision of the taxable service of construction which has been re-defined by clause (zzq) of sub-section (105) of section 65 to read as ‘commercial or industrial construction service’. It has been explained in the below mentioned paragraph 5.

Taxable service of construction

5. Clause (zzq) of sub-section (105) of section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 originally inserted by Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 explained the meaning of the taxable service of construction as a service provided ‘to any person, by a commercial concern, in relation to construction service’. However, Finance Act, 2005 has amended this meaning to read as a service provided ‘to any person, by a commercial concern, in relation to commercial or industrial construction service.’ The expression ‘commercial or industrial construction service’ has been explained in paragraph 6 infra.

5.1 Definition of ‘construction service’ has been made more specific - The original definition of ‘construction service’ as introduced by Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 was general in nature. However, Finance Act, 2005 has made it more specific to cover commercial and industrial construction services only, thus excluding the services for personal use.

5.2 Revised definition of ‘construction services’ is inclusive and not exhaustive - Thus, from the meaning of the taxable construction service as given above, it is quite evident that the residential complex, which is the subject-matter of service tax, should be used only for commercial or industrial use. In other words, the residential complexes which are not intended for commercial or industrial use or are intended for personal use would not be subjected to service tax. Moreover, the meaning of ‘construction services’ as expanded by Finance Act, 2005 to read as ‘commercial or industrial construction service’ is wide enough and is inclusive in nature and not exhaustive. Besides the construction of residential complexes, certain other construction services, which have been pointed out in paragraph No. 22 infra, are also to be read with the expanded definition of construction services so that they are covered under ‘commercial or industrial construction services’ to attract service tax.

5.3 Services not specifically mentioned may also be subjected to service tax due to the revised definition of ‘construction services’ - Not only those services which have been specifically mentioned in paragraph No. 22 infra, other services which may be treated as commercial or industrial construction service would also attract service tax as per the revised definition of construction services; since the definition is inclusive and not exhaustive.

The developer provides a package of services which attract service tax. Again, the developer cannot escape the liability to service tax merely because he remains owner till the completion of the construction, for the ultimate fact is that the applicant does everything to honour its commitment to the customer from whom he receives valuable consideration in instalments. Only that construction gets excluded from the purview of residential complex and from service tax net where a complex is constructed by a person directly engaging the services of any other person for designing or planning of the layout, and after completion of construction, it is meant to be used for residential purpose either by him or his lessee or a person permitted by him. This ‘excluding clause’ cannot be applied in case of a developer merely because the ownership and possession, for the time being, vests in him. After construction is completed, the ownership and possession will be transferred to the other persons who have booked the complexes, which implies that the developer is providing services of constructing residential complexes to the other party. RAJAT MOHAN

CA

Introduction to the case

1. Builders challenged and prayed for quashing of part of Notification No. 15/2004-ST, dated 10th September, 2004 and Notification No. 18/2005-ST, dated 7th June, 2005 and Notification No. 1/2006-ST, dated 1st March, 2006. Said notifications levied service tax in respect of construction carried out under 'works contract' prior to introduction of specific service.

2. Issues

2.1 Whether Levy of service tax on composite contracts was valid even prior to introduction of works contract services?

2.2 Whether abatement Notification No. 15/2004-ST, Notification No. 18/2005-ST and Notification No. 1/2006-ST providing for optional abatement are valid?

3. Petitioner's contention

(i)

Service tax was applicable only in respect of service element and the Central Government did not have any power under the residual entry to impose tax on entries under List II of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. In other words, Central Government could not impose service tax on material or goods used in execution of works/composite contract.

(ii)

Section 65(105)(zzq) and (zzzh) of the Finance Act, 1994 applied only to "service contracts" and not to, "composite or works contract", therefore, Abatement Notification (67%) was contrary to the charging provision and a nullity, as it amounted to enlarging and widening of charging section. They also contended that a notification could not expand or enlarge the charging section or even amend the statutory provisions or the main enactment.

(iii)

Subsequent legislation showed that the earlier legislation would not cover "composite or works contract". They also contended that vagueness or uncertainty made a levy invalid and illegal.

Department's Contention

4. It was argued by Department that the abatement notifications in question were optional and an assessee needed not take benefit of the said notifications, if he so desired, but the service tax was to be levied and was payable on the service component of a composite contract, which could be computed. The notifications also specifically stipulated, pre-conditions which had to be satisfied in totality before any benefit under them could be taken.

Court of Law

5. While delivering the path breaking judgment the Hon'ble High Court explained the history of service tax in this matter and stated that Service tax had been imposed in three stages. In the first stage, service tax was imposed on construction of industrial and commercial complexes. In the second stage, service tax was imposed on residential complexes of 12 or more residential units and in the third stage, service tax was imposed on works contracts.

Each provision or levy had its own scope and ambit-while the first two provisions were primarily specific and targeted, the third inclusion, i.e., works contract was very broad and wide term and included within its ambit and scope construction of industrial and commercial complex or construction of residential complexes as specified.

Court also stated that introduction and imposition of service tax on works contract by the Finance Act, 2007 would not mean that we had to read down enacted tax levy. The new amendment by Finance Act, 2007 did not indicate that works contract relating to "construction of industrial and commercial complexes" or "construction of complexes", would be only applicable when the contractor was providing labour or service and was paid for the same and not to composite contracts.

Taxable Service

2. ‘Construction of Complex services’ was brought in the ambit of service tax by the Finance Act, 2005. As per section 65(105)( zzzh) of the Finance Act, 1994 (‘the Act’), taxable service means any service provided or to be provided to any person, by any other person, in relation to construction of complex.

Section 65(30a) of the Act reads as under :

‘construction of complex’ means

"(a )construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof; or

(b )completion and finishing services in relation to residential complex such as glazing, plastering, painting, floor and wall tiling, wall covering and wall papering, wood and metal joinery and carpentry, fencing and railing, construction of swimming pools, acoustic applications or fittings and other similar services; or

(c )repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services in relation to, residential complex;"

Section 65(91a) reads as follows :

‘residential complex’ means any complex comprising of—

"(i )a building or buildings, having more than twelve residential units;

(ii )a common area; and

(iii )any one or more of facilities or services such as park, lift, parking space, community hall, common water supply or effluent treatment system,

located within a premises and the layout of such premises is approved by any authority under any law for the time being in force, but does not include a complex which is constructed by a person directly engaging any other person for designing or planning of the layout, and the construction of such complex is intended for personal use as residence by such person.

Explanation.—For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that for the purposes of this clause,—

(a )‘personal use’ includes permitting the complex for use as residence by another person on rent or without consideration;

(b )‘residential unit’ means a single house or a single apartment intended for use as a place of residence;"

Service tax Applicability

3. As per the Central Board of Excise & Customs vide Circular No. 96/7 of 2007 (Reference Code: 079.01), dated August 23, 2007, the promoters/developers engaged in the building construction normally should carry out their activities either—

(a)by entering into a contract with one or more independent contractor(s) for execution of the entire construction, or

(b)with the help of a person directly engaging any other person for designing or planning of the layout.

In case of the former (a) the sub-contractor(s) are liable for payment of service tax and in later (b) case, there is no service tax leviable.

If no other person is engaged for construction work and the builder/promoter/developer/any such person undertakes construction work on his own without engaging the services of any other person, then in such cases,

(i)service provider and service recipient relationship does not exist,

(ii)services provided are in the nature of self-supply of services.

In the absence of service provider and service recipient relationship, if the service provided is in the nature of self-supply of service, the question of providing taxable service to any person by any other person does not arise. Thus, no service tax on construction of residential flat is levied if the builder has constructed the flats on his own.

The necessary condition, however, remains that the promoter/developer continues to be the owner of the complex and in the event of selling, he becomes the service provider and is liable to pay service tax.

Valuation

Valuation of the services would be at the transaction value. However, valuation with the related parties/ between various group companies needs to be properly dealt with and must be kept at the arm's length price to avoid unnecessary departmental intrusion.

However, one major change has been done in the valuation provisions in GST. In real estate sector, generally customer delays in making to the payment to the developers. Many times, the developer charges interest on such delayed payment. Such interest is outside the scope of tax net presently as no tax is charged on such interest whether it be VAT, Service Tax or Excise Duty. However, in GST regime, such interest will be included in the transaction value of supply and accordingly GST will be levied on such interest. Further, builder will need to bifurcate the interest on basic construction amount and amount of other services like PLC etc. as interest on basic amount will be chargeable at the rate of 12% (i.e. rate of main supply) and interest on other services at 18%.

Treatment of cancellations of bookings

In real estate sector, cancellations of bookings of flats/shops etc. is a very prevalent and common practice. Since the delivery period of a project is very high often extending to several years, many customers cancel their bookings of flats during the project.

Presently, developers can issue credit note and take benefit under Rule 6(3) of Service Tax Rules, 1994, in regard to the tax paid earlier on a cancelled booking when such booking is cancelled. Similar provisions exist in VAT laws also.

Same concept has been kept in GST regime, wherein a person can issue a credit note in case of cancellation of a service and take benefit of the tax paid earlier on such service. However, as per Section 34 of CGST Act, 2017, such credit note have to be shown/declared in the return of the month when such note is issued. However, there is a restriction which says that such credit note can be shown only up to in the return for the month of September of the following financial year in which supply is made.

Illustration

Suppose a supply was made in the month of August, 2017(F.Y. 2017-18). If a credit note is issued against this transaction, it can be shown in any return up to return of the month of September' 2018 (F.Y. 2018-19). However, if any credit note is issued after this date, it cannot be shown in return and therefore, its benefit cannot be taken.

This provision is going to pose a major hurdle for real estate sector because the construction projects usually take several years to complete. Therefore, various customers book their flats and then cancels the booking several many months/years later. However, the benefit will be available only for a selected period and would pose a very troublesome issue.

Exemption for construction industry withdrawn

Earlier, in service tax, Central Government has provided many construction service related exemption like construction of canal, dams, road, affordable housing projects etc. But, with the introduction of GST regime, government is looking to end this Exemption-Raj of service tax for many construction related services. Now, in GST, only pure labour contracts entered for house construction under Housing for All(Urban) Mission/Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY) and labour contracts used in construction of single residential unit otherwise than as a part of residential complex are kept exempt as per draft exemption list released by the GST council.

Major impact will be on affordable housing projects which are currently exempt from service tax and have not been kept in the exemption list of GST.

Flow of credits

In present regime, a Builder opting for Abatement under Notification No. 26/2012-ST is not eligible for CENVAT credit of inputs (Excise Duty). In GST regime, all the above duties/taxes (except stamp duty) will get subsumed, therefore a builder will be able to avail the input tax credit of all its procurement of goods/services. Therefore, it would reduce the tax costs substantially in the construction industry. Under GST, it is expected that seamless credit of all taxes paid on procurement of goods/ services will be allowed so that net outflow of GST liability would be minimized.

23.1-8 Redevelopment is subject to GST

In both the cases, GST is payable as in first case, the promoter receives consideration in form of TDR and in other cases, by cash.

22.6 Distinction between construction service and works contract service

There is no doubt that construction contract is also a 'works contract'. However, under GST, distinction has been made between 'works contract service' and 'construction of complex'.

The distinction is that in case of works contract, a customer (recipient of supply of service) approaches the supplier of service (contractor) to undertake construction as per his requirements. In almost all the cases, the land is owned by or taken on lease by customer. The contractor enters into contract with customer and then undertakes construction with his own material. If the material is supplied by recipient himself (customer), then it is not works contract. It is simple contract for work.

In construction of complex, the builder or developer normally does not have any identified customer. Even if he has some identified customers before commencement of construction, he is undertaking construction activity on his own and not on basis of contract with customer. The land never belongs to the customer.

What is written below is not what is actually written against Sr Nos. 41A and 41B but what is actually meant (based on principles). Hope the notification will be amended suitably to clarify the position.

As per the principle, the first step is to calculate GST payable on development rights transferred, which pertain to residential apartments.

(A) GST on transfer of development rights/FST attributable residential apartments = GST payable on TDR or FSI (including additional FSI) or both or on upfront amount payable in respect of service by way of granting of long term lease of thirty years, or more for construction of the project] × (carpet area of the residential apartments in the project) ÷ (Total carpet area of the residential and commercial apartments in the project) .

[The notification wrongly terms it as 'Amount of exemption available for construction of residential apartments].

The second step is to calculate GST payable by promoter on un-booked residential apartments.

The promoter shall be liable to pay tax at the applicable rate, on reverse charge basis, on such proportion of value of development rights or FSI (Including additional FSI) or both, or upfront amount (called as premium, salami, cost, price, development charges or by any other name) paid for long term lease of land, as is attributable to the residential apartments, which remain un-booked on the date of issuance of completion certificate, or first occupation of the project, as the case may be.

The calculation will be made in the following manner -

(B) GST payable on residential apartments remain un-booked on date of completion = [GST payable on TDR or FSI (including additional FSI) or both or upfront amount (called as premium, salami, cost, price, development charges or by any other name) payable for long term lease of land for construction of the residential apartments in the project but for the exemption contained herein] × (carpet area of the residential apartments in the project which remain un-booked on the date of issuance of completion certificate or first occupation÷ Total carpet area of the residential apartments in the project) - first proviso to Sr Nos. 41A and 41B of Notification No. 12/2019-CT (Rate) dated 28-6-2017 inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2019.

The exemption available on transfer of development rights/FSI attributable to residential apartments which were booked prior to date of completion = (A) - (B).

Real Estate Services relating to residential and commercial apartments

23.1 Background

Taxation of real estate sector has always been problematic issue. The major reason is that the sector is still unorganized. The complications started after introduction of State tax on works contract. The problem aggravated after introduction of service tax on works contract.

The State tax and Service tax was merged on introduction of GST w.e.f. 1-7-2017. However, many issues were still unresolved.

Hence, the GST structure on real estate services relating to residential and commercial apartments has been thoroughly altered w.e.f. 1-4-2019.

This service falls under service code 9954.

The highlights of revised scheme are as follows -

The revised scheme applies to residential and commercial apartments which are covered under RERA [Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016].

The provisions do not apply to construction of single houses or works contracts not covered under RERA.

The new scheme is compulsory for projects commenced on or after 1-4-2019. In respect of ongoing projects as on 31-3-2019, the promoter has option to shift to new scheme w.e.f. 1-4-2019 (without ITC) or continue under earlier scheme (with ITC)

Under new scheme, the GST rates for residential apartments are as follows - (a) CGST 0.5% plus SGST/UTGST 0.5% (total 1%) or IGST 1% (without ITC) for affordable residential apartments (b) CGST 2.5% plus SGST/UTGST 2.5% (total 5%) or IGST 5% (without ITC) for other residential apartments, where price includes value of land.

In respect of commercial apartments (shops, offices, godowns etc.) in RREP, the GST rate is CGST 2.5% plus SGST/UTGST 2.5% (total 5%) or IGST 5% (without ITC). In respect of construction of commercial apartments (other than RREP), the GST rate is CGST 6% plus SGST/UTGST 6% (total 12%) or IGST 12% (with ITC).

In case of ongoing projects, if the promoter intends to shift to new scheme (of 1%/5%) w.e.f. 1-4-2019, he is required to refund excess ITC availed as on 31-3-2019 or get credit of ITC less claimed as on 31-3-2019.

RREP (Residential Real Estate Project) means Real Estate Project (REP) of residential apartments with commercial apartments not more than 15% of total carpet area of REP.

Affordable Residential Apartment means apartment having carpet area not exceeding 60 square meter in metropolitan cities or 90 square meter in cities or towns other than metropolitan cities and for which the gross amount charged is not more than Rs. 45 lakhs.

These rates apply where supply of services involves transfer of land or undivided share of land and its charges are included in the amount charged to customer.

In respect of new projects, the tax (CGST, SGST/UTGST or IGST as applicable) shall be paid in cash by debiting the electronic cash ledger only [without utilising Input Tax Credit].

In case of ongoing projects as on 1-4-2019, the promoter has option to opt for earlier provisions of tax i.e. with utilization of ITC. If promoter intends to continue under old scheme, he has to submit declaration in specified form to jurisdictional Commissioner before 20-5-2019.

If the promoter does not submit such declaration, he is deemed to have opted for the new scheme.

If landowner- promoter transfers development right or FSI (including additional FSI) to a promoter (developer- promoter) against consideration, wholly or partly, in the form of construction of apartments, the developer- promoter shall pay tax on supply of construction of apartments to the landowner-promoter. The landowner - promoter can take credit of taxes charged from him by the developer promoter, if the landowner-promoter further supplies such apartments to his buyers.

No GST is payable where the entire consideration has been received after issuance of completion certificate, where required, by the competent authority or after its first occupation, whichever is earlier.

22.3-1 Works Contract is supply of service for rate of tax under GST

Works contract as defined in section 2(119) of CGST Act is a composite supply and shall be treated as 'supply of service' - Para 6(a) of Schedule II of CGST Act.

General rate of GST on composite supply of works contract services is 18%. This is irrespective of GST rate on individual goods used in execution of works contract.

Works Contract is deemed sale of goods as per Constitution - A tax on the transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of a works contract is deemed sale of goods under Article 366(29A) of Constitution of India. [Note that this Article in the Constitution of India is continuing even after Constitutional amendment].

Works contract is not limited to construction - The term 'works contract' is not limited to construction services. It covers all activities relating to plant, machinery or equipment which are immovable.

22.3-2 Works contract service of renewable energy plant and equipment

General rate on works contract services is 18%. If composite contract of supply of goods plus service of construction, installation, commissioning of renewable energy plant is executed, it becomes works contract and GST rate becomes 18% on whole contract. Thus, whole purpose of promoting renewable energy sources gets defeated.

Hence, it is provided that in case of such composite contract, value of goods will be taken as 70% and GST rate will be 5%. Value of services will be 30% attracting GST @ 18%. The provisions are as follows -

Service provider can opt to pay service tax on value of services. However, if he is unable to compute the value of services, he can pay service tax under composition scheme. Till 1-3-2013, the rate applicable was 25% in all above cases].

Amount to include fair market value of material supplied by service receiver - The amount charged shall be the sum total of the amount charged for the service including the fair market value of all goods and services supplied by the recipient(s) in or in relation to the service, whether or not supplied under the same contract or any other contract. From the fair market value, following can be deduced - (i) the amount charged for such goods or services supplied to the service provider, if any; and (ii) the value added tax or sales tax, if any, levied thereon. The fair market value of goods and services so supplied may be determined in accordance with the generally accepted accounting principles.

Thus, if the customer has supplied some material by charging for the same, its amount can be deducted including Vat/Sales tax.

For example, fair market value of material supplied by service receiver is Rs. one lakh and the service receiver, instead of supplying the material free, has charged the service provider Rs. 60,000 plus Rs. 3,000 as Vat, Rs. one lakh will be added to the amount charged by service provider and deduction of Rs. 63,000 will be given. In effect, Rs. 37,000 will be added.

The provision of adding value of free supplied material to contractor (service provider) has been held invalid in Bhayana Builders v. CST (2013) 42 GST 76 = 38 taxmann.com 221 (CESTAT LB). In my view, this decision cannot apply in respect of services provided after 1-7-2012. See discussions under Works Contract Service.

Inclusions/exclusions of other amounts collected by builder/developer from customer - Preferential Location Charges (PLC), additional charges for modifications suggested by customers, maintenance during construction period, covered parking charges etc. These are naturally bundled services and should get covered under construction of complex' and be eligible for abatement in valuation.

The builder collects some charges like External Development Charges etc. which are payable to Government authorities. However, this is actually liability of builder himself. He does not act as pure agent of the customer. These should be includible in value of service but should be eligible for abatement.

However, club membership fee is not part of construction service and cannot get covered under 'naturally bundled service'. Similarly, maintenance service provided after construction is over is not part of construction service and should not be eligible for abatement.

If the builder/developer collects some amounts on actual basis, such as deposits for some activities like society membership, electricity deposit and connection charges for handing over to concerned authorities, it can be said that he is acting as pure agent of the customer and these are not includible in value.

REAL ESTATE SECTOR AND RIGHTS OF INVESTORS

There has been an unprecedented growth in demand for real estate across all markets in recent years making the exercise dearer though the industry is definitely having troubled times now because of Covid. This unprecedented growth earlier was attributed in no small measure to the vibrant economy, robust growth and resultant housing demand exceeding supply. Realizing the importance of accounting for construction contracts, the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India had revised Accounting Standard 7 with effect from 1st April, 2003.

Realizing the potential of the housing sector, amendments to section 65(30a) in the Finance Act 1994 were made in defining "Construction of Complex".

Amendments were made to section 65(91a) of the Finance Act 1994 to the definition of "Residential Complex"

(a)

"Construction of Complex" means -

(i)

construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof; or

(ii)

completion and finishing services in relation to residential complex such as glazing, plastering, painting, floor and wall tiling, wall covering and wall papering, wood and metal joinery and carpentry, fencing and railing, construction of swimming pools, acoustic applications or fittings and other similar services; or

(iii)

repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services in relation to, residential complex;

[Section 65(30a) of the Finance Act, 1994]

(b)

"Residential Complex" means any complex comprising of—

(i)

a building or buildings, having more than twelve residential units;

(ii)

a common area; and

(iii)

any one or more of facilities or services such as park, lift, parking space, community hall, common water supply or effluent treatment system, located within a premises and the layout of such premises is approved by an authority under any law for the time being in force, but does not include a complex which is constructed by a person directly engaging any other person for designing or planning of the layout, and the construction of such complex is intended for personal use as residence by such person.

Explanation - For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that for the purposes of this clause,

(i)

personal use includes permitting the complex for use as residence by another person on rent or without consideration;

(ii)

residential unit means a single house or a single apartment intended for use as a place of residence;

[Section 65(91a) of the Finance Act, 1994]

Section 65(105)(zzzh) of the Finance Act 1994, as amended, provided for levy of service tax on services provided to any person by any other person in relation to construction of complex.

The amendments to section 65(105) of the Finance Act, 1994 were introduced by the Finance Act 2005 and the amendments were brought into force with effect from 16-6-2005 vide Notification No.15/2005 dated 07.06.2005. Prior to 16-6-2005 there was no service tax on constructions of new residential blocks.

The VAT laws were also applicable to the construction industry particularly the levy of Tax on transfer of property in goods involved in execution of Works Contracts. Rules and regulations pertaining to labour enactments were applicable if the total number of employees exceeded the specified number. Apart from labour laws, business laws were also applicable.

VAT laws were replaced by GST Act with effect from 1-7-2017.

Under the CGST Act, 2017 there is only one taxable event i.e., Supply.

"Goods and Services Tax" means "any tax on supply of goods or services or both except tax on supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption [Article 366(12A) of the Constitutional (101st Amendment) Act, 2016]".

Supply includes sale, transfer, exchange, barter, license, rental, lease and disposal. If a person undertakes any of these transactions during the course or furtherance of business for consideration, it will be covered under the meaning of Supply under GST. [Section 7 of the CGST Act 2017]

Section 7 of the CGST Act 2017 was amended to include a new clause under the definition of supply. Activities or transactions involving the supply of goods or services by any person, other than an individual, to its members or constituents or vice versa, for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration. Earlier this supply would have been considered as only supply of goods under Schedule II of the CGST Act. So, the scope is expanded now for levy.

29.9-2 Renting of precincts of a religious place exempt upto limit

Renting of precincts of a religious place meant for general public, owned by charitable or religious trust are exempt from GST.

However, this exemption does not apply to - (i) renting of rooms where charges are one thousand rupees or more per day; (ii) renting of premises, community halls, kalyan mandapam or open area, and the like where charges are ten thousand rupees or more per day (iii) renting of shops or other spaces for business or commerce where charges are ten thousand rupees or more per month - Notification No. 12/2017-CT (Rate) and No. 9/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017, effective from 1-7-2017.

Meaning of 'general public' - "General public" means the body of people at large sufficiently defined by some common quality of public or impersonal nature - Definition clause 2(zc) of Notification No. 12/2017-CT (Rates) and 9/2017-IT (Rates) both dated 28-6-2017, effective from 1-7-2017.

Public Place - Public Place means any place intended to be used by or accessible to the public and includes any public conveyance. It is not necessary that it must be public property. Even if it is a private property, it is sufficient that the place is accessible to the public - Gaurav Jain v. UOI AIR 1997 SC 3021 - quoted and followed in JGS Enterprises v. CCE (2018) 66 GST 599 = 92 taxmann.com 2 (CESTAT).

The word 'precincts' has very broad meaning - CBE&C vide circular No. 200/10/2016-ST dated 6-9-2016 had clarified that the word 'precincts' has very broad meaning. All immovable property located in the immediate vicinity and surrounding of the religious place and owned by religious place or under same management as the religious place may be considered as 'precincts' of the religious place.

The word 'precinct' has to be given broad meaning. It means surrounding region or area. -South Eastern Coalfields v. CCE (2006) 200 ELT 357 (SC).

An occupancy certificate (OC), issued by the local authorities, certifies that a building is fit for occupation and has been constructed as per the approved plan and in compliance with local law.

There are 3 different certificates issued at successive short periods and these are explained below-

(i)

Completion Certificate-The concerned authorities would issue a completion certificate (CC) to a housing project, after ensuring that all requirements with regard to the project is complete so that it is suitable for habitation. It is only after a CC is issued to a project that it becomes ready for possession for home buyers.

(ii)

Occupancy Certificate- An OC, on the other hand, is a certificate stating that the project has been built in accordance with all construction norms, building bye-laws, etc. It is only after a project receives an OC, can the builder apply for various utilities for the project and.

Possession Certificate-A possession certificate is issued to the buyer by the developer, as proof of transfer of ownership. It mentions the date of possession of the property by the new buyer. Clause 5(b) of the Schedule II of CGST Act, 2017 stipulates that "Construction of a complex, building, civil structure or a part thereof, including a complex or building intended for sale to a buyer, wholly or partly" shall be treated as supply of service except where the entire consideration was received after issuance of completion certificate.

In other words, if any consideration is received before issuance of completion certificate involving the construction of a complex, building, civil structure intended for sale to a buyer then it will be considered as supply of a service, liable for GST and if the whole consideration is paid by the Buyer after the issuance of occupancy certificate or first occupancy, whichever is earlier, then it will be outside the GST implications i.e. no GST will be imposable.

29.8 Leasing of mines of petroleum crude or natural gas

Licensing services for right to use minerals including its exploration and evaluation fall under service code 997337.

Leasing of mines of petroleum crude or natural gas - Service of leasing of mines of petroleum crude or natural gas is a taxable service. The partial exemption is available as explained below.

The intra-State supply and inter-State of services by way of grant of license or lease to explore or mine petroleum crude or natural gas or both is exempt from so much of the CGST or IGST as is leviable on the consideration paid to the Central Government in the form of Central Government's share of profit petroleum as defined in the contract entered into by the Central Government in this behalf - Notification No. 5/2017-CT (Rate) and No. 5/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 25-1-2018.

29.9 Real Estate Leasing and Renting Services

Renting or leasing services fall under group 99721. The GST rate is 18% (9% CGST and 9% SGST). Since place of supply is location of immovable property, IGST is not leviable.

Limited coverage of real estate services in GST - The definition of 'service' is very wide at it covers anything other than 'goods'. However, para 5 of Schedule III of CGST Act States that activity of sale of land and subject to para 5(b) of Schedule II, sale of buildings is neither supply of goods nor supply of services.

Para 5(b) of Schedule II covers sale of a flat or commercial premises in a complex.

As per Entry No. 49 of List II of Seventh Schedule to Constitution, 'taxes on lands and buildings' is a State subject.

Though Constitution grants concurrent powers to Union and State to levy GST, these are subject to recommendation of GST Council. Thus, GST on land and buildings can be imposed only to the extent recommended by GST Council.

In respect of land and buildings, the CGST Act and SGST Act makes some 'deeming provisions' in Schedule II of CGST Act.

Thus, excluding those 'deemed supply' provisions, GST cannot be imposed on other transactions relating to land and buildings.

1.3-9 Tax on entertainment only by Municipalities, panchayat, regional council and district council

Municipality, panchayat, Regional Council and District Council will have powers to impose tax on entertainment and amusement [Entry 62 of List II (State List) of Seventh Schedule to Constitution of India as amended w.e.f. 16-9-2016]. District Councils for administration of Tribal Areas in States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram will have powers to impose entertainment tax [paragraph 8(3)(d) of Sixth Schedule to Constitution of India inserted w.e.f. 16-9-2016].

State Government can impose luxury tax on Cable TV operators - State of Kerala v. Asianet Satellite Communications Ltd. (2025) 30 Centax 436 (SC) [This judgment is not much relevant under GST].

1.4 Rates of GST

The IGST and CGST Acts do not indicate GST rate structure.

As per section 9 of CGST Act, rate of CGST will be as notified by Central/State Government. The rate shall not exceed 20%. Same provision will be in SGST Act of each State.

Thus, total GST rate for intra-State supplies will not exceed 40% [20% CGST and 20% SGST].

As per section 5 of IGST Act, rate of IGST will be as notified by Central Government. The rate shall not exceed 40%.

CGST and IGST rates will be common all over India. SGST rates are also expected to be common all over India. However, since State Governments have sovereign powers to levy GST, the SGST rates may vary from State to State, though presently they are same.

UTGST Rates will be same as CGST Rates as these rates are within jurisdiction of Central Government.

The GST rates on goods are notified based on Customs Tariff Act, which is based on HSN Code. However, though Customs Tariff has eight digit code, only first four digits are used to notify GST rates. Thus, in many cases, for same four digit item, GST rates may vary depending on description of goods.

In case of services, service classification code is a 6 digit code. First two digits are always '99'.
