22.2-4 Plant & machinery assembled at site is works contract and hence 'supply of service'

Plant and Machinery or structure assembled and erected at site is 'works contract'.

The word 'goods' applies to those which can be brought to market for being bought and sold, and it is implied that it applies to such goods as are movable. Goods erected and installed in the premises and embedded to earth cease to be goods and cannot be held to be excisable goods. - Quality Steel Tubes (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 75 ELT 17 = (1995) 2 SCC 372 = 1995 AIR SCW 11 - in this case, it was held that tube mill and welding head erected and installed in the premises and embedded in the earth for manufacture of steel tubes and pipes are not 'goods'.

In Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Indian Oil Corporation AIR 1991 SC 686 = 1991 Supp (2) SCC 18, it was held that if the chattel is movable to another place in the same position (condition?), it is movable property. If it has to be dismantled and re-erected at later place, it is attached to earth and is immovable property - followed in Triveni Engineering v. CCE 2000 AIR SCW 3144 = 40 RLT 1 = 120 ELT 273 (SC), where it was observed, 'The marketability test requires that the goods as such should be in a position to be taken to market and sold. If they have to be separated, the test is not satisfied'.

Explanation.—For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that for the purposes of this clause,— (a )‘personal use’ includes permitting the complex for use as residence by other person on rent or without consideration;

(b )‘residential unit’ means a single house or a single apartment intended for use as place of residence;"

According to the definition given above, the following are the ingredients of the term ‘residential complex’

uthe complex must have twelve residential units in a building or buildings

uit must have a common area

uit must have one or more amenities such as parking space, park, etc.

uit must be situated within a single premises, i.e., it must be all together

uthe layout of the complex has to be approved by the authority under law e.g. municipal corporation, gram panchayat, etc., (because of this clause, illegal slums will never come under tax net since they do not have any layout approved by authority)

All these ingredients are necessary to constitute a residential complex. If one of these ingredients is missing then, even though that may be termed as complex, it will not be chargeable to service tax. But if we see the ingredients carefully we can find that the builder who is building a complex has to provide majority of the above-referred facilities. Moreover parking space which is mentioned in sub-clause (iii) is now-a-days mandatory. The important point is that the complex should have building or buildings having twelve residential units. Therefore, it is clear that the individual buildings having less than twelve residential units are not covered under the service tax net. But if these buildings are situated in one area and stand as a society, then they will be considered altogether and will get covered under the tax net since the total residential units are twelve or more than twelve, provided other requirements of residential complex are fulfilled.

‘Personal use’ - Meaning of

4. The definition of residential complex also specifically excludes complexes which are developed by engaging other person for designing or planning the layout and which are used for personal use as residence. For this purpose, the term ‘personal use’ is defined as

"‘personal use’ includes permitting the complex for use as residence by another person on rent or without consideration;"

Because of the above definition, ‘personal use’ not only includes self use but also used by any other person as a tenant or by any other person without any consideration, i.e. , free of charge. But this use also has to be for residence only.

What is a ‘residential unit’

5. It is important to note that the term ‘residential unit’ mentioned in the definition of ‘residential complex’ is very important. Therefore, the Legislature has taken efforts to define the same. It has defined it in the Explanation to the residential complex definition, which is as follows :

"‘residential unit’ means a single house or a single apartment intended for use as a place of residence;"

From above definition, it can be seen that residential unit is nothing but an apartment or a house that is intended to be used as a place of residence. Now because of the term ‘house’, a society having twelve row houses and other requisites of residential complex as mentioned in its definition may get covered under the service tax net.

After considering all the relevant legal provisions relating to this category of service one would appreciate that the end use must be for residence and not for any other purpose. It is, therefore, clear that the construction of complex, intended to be used for residence, is only taxable under this category of service.

Taxable service

6. The ‘taxable’ service for this category is defined in sub-clause (zzh) of clause (105) of section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 as—

"to any person, by any person, in relation to construction of complex,"

Therefore, any person who provides service in relation to construction of complex to any person is taxable under this category.

No. 3 and hence the services of construction of residential apartments in the project rendered by the applicant do not qualify for the concessional rate of tax of 12 per cent under any of the sub-tems or items of Sl. No. 3 of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. Therefore, the services of construction of all different types of residential apartments in the project is liable to GST at the rate of 18 per cent [ 9 per cent CGST + 9 per cent SGST] as per Item (I) of Sl. No. 3 of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. [Para 8]

The second question raised by the applicant is regarding the taxable value of services for the period 1-7-2017 onwards for which appropriation towards undivided share of land was already done in pre-GST period and whether the one-third deduction as provided for in para 2 of Notification No. 11/2017 can again be taken where the value of undivided share already appropriated is lower than one-third of the total amount receivable for project including land value. On a plain reading of provision of para 2 of Notification No. 11/2017, it is evident that the taxable value of service specified at Item (i) of the said notification is the total amount charged for the supply less the value of land or undivided share of land and the value of land or undivided share of land shall be deemed to be one third of the total amount charged for the supply. Therefore, the value of land or undivided share of land is deemed to be one-third of the total amount charged for the supply irrespective of the actual value of land and, accordingly, the applicant is eligible to avail deduction of one-third of the total amount charged for the supply in arriving at the taxable value of the supply. [Para 9]

The third question raised by the applicant is regarding the applicable rate of tax for the period after 1-4-2019 where option was already exercised in respect of the apartments mentioned therein and eligibility for one-third deduction to the extent consideration for undivided share of land is also included. Consequent to the introduction of the new tax structure for real estate sector with effect from 1-4-2019 onwards by amendment of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 by Notification No. 3/2019 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 29-3-2019 the applicant has opted for continuing payment of tax at the old rates that have been specified in item (ie) or (if) of the said notification in respect of the services of construction of residential apartments in the ongoing project. The project does not come under any of the schemes specified in item (ie) of the said notification and accordingly the services of construction of the residential apartments in the project is liable to GST for the period from 1-4-2019 at the rate of 18 per cent [9 per cent CGST + 9 per cent SGST] as per item (if) of Sl. No. 3 of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended by Notification No. 3/2019 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 29-3-2019 in accordance with the option exercised by the applicant. The item (if) of Sl. No. 3 of the said notification provides that the provisions of paragraph 2 of the notification shall apply for valuation of the service. Therefore, the applicant is eligible for deduction of one-third of the total amount charged for the supply in determining the taxable value of such supply after 1-4-2019 also. [Para 10]

The respondent was executing an affordable Housing Scheme approved by the Government of Haryana under the name and style of 'Arawali Homes'.

An application was filed before the Haryana State Screening Committee on Anti-Profiteering alleging profiteering by the respondent in respect of purchase of a flat in the respondent's project 'Arawali Homes'. The applicant had alleged that the respondent was collecting wrong GST post-implementation of GST and was not refunding GST collected in the wrong manner, even after sending clarification that the GST was not applicable to 'Affordable Housing', as the GST amount could be adjusted against the Input Tax Credit (ITC).

The DGAP noted that the ITC as a percentage of the turnover that was available to the respondent during the pre-GST period from April, 2016 to June, 2017 was 2.42 per cent and during the post-GST period from July, 2017 to August, 2018, it was 10.70 per cent which clearly established that post-GST, the respondent had benefited from additional ITC to the tune of 8.28 per cent [10.70 per cent (-) 2.42 per cent] of the taxable turnover. The effective GST rate on construction service in respect of the affordable and low-cost houses upto a carpet area of 60 square metres was further reduced from 12 per cent to 8 per cent, vide Notification No. 1/2018-Central Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018.

Entry No. 3(v)(da) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 is related to the construction of low-cost apartments. Clause (xvi) of Paragraph 4 of the Rate Notification defines an affordable residential apartment. It shall mean a residential apartment in a project which commences on or after 1-4-2019 or in an ongoing project in respect of which the promoter has not exercised the option to pay tax at the rate specified in (ie) or (if) of Entry No. 3, having carpet area not exceeding 60 sq. mtr. in metropolitan cities or 90 sq. mtr. In cities or towns other than metropolitan cities and for which the gross amount charged is not more than 45 lakhs. [Para 4.1]

The flats having a carpet area of 60 sq. mtr. or less per unit in the RREP qualify as affordable residential apartments, provided the gross amount charged per unit does not exceed Rs. 45 lakhs and the promoter has not exercised the option to pay tax at the rate specified in (ie) or (if) of Entry No. 3. It now needs to be ascertained whether the RREP is an affordable housing project, which enjoys infrastructure status vide the AHP Notification. [Para 4.6]

Affordable housing has been defined in the AHP Notification as a housing project using at least 50 per cent of FAR/FSI for dwelling units with a carpet area of not more than 60 sq. mtr. The term 'carpet area' has been assigned the same meaning as in section 2(k) of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016. It means the net usable floor area of an apartment, excluding the area covered by the external walls, areas under services shafts, balcony or veranda and open terrace, but includes the area covered by the internal partition walls of the apartment. [Para 4.7]

The Floor Area Ratio (FAR), also known as the Floor Space Ratio (FSR) or the Floor Space Index (FSI), depicts the relationship between the total usable floor space in a building and the total area of the plot on which the building is constructed. In mathematical terms, FAR = CA/LA, where CA = Constructed area or built-up area, and LA = Land area. [Para 4.8]

According to the Project Plan submitted at the time of the hearing, FAR for the entire project is 2.749 after deducting from the total built-up area the common areas like lift-lobby, stair area etc. FAR for the affordable residential apartments in the project should, therefore, be atleast 1.375. The total plot size being 5627 sq. mtr., the built-up area for affordable residential apartments should atleast be 7734 sq. mtr. The built-up area for the affordable residential apartments, as identified by the architect, under the RREP is 7885 sq. mtr. (the calculation sheet is attached). The relevant FAR, therefore, comes out to be 1.401, which is 50.96 per cent of the FAR for the project. The RREP, therefore, is an affordable housing project in terms of the AHP Notification. [Para 4.9]

Thus, it is concluded that the works contract service for the construction of those dwelling units in the RREP that are affordable residential apartments in terms of clause (xvi) of Paragraph 4 of the Rate Notification are taxable under Entry No. 3(v)(da) of the said notification, provided the applicant does not opt for paying tax at the rate specified in (ie) or (if) of Entry No. 3. [Para 4.10]

Thus, the works contract service for the construction of those dwelling units in the project named 'Akriti' that are affordable residential apartments in terms of clause (xvi) of Paragraph 4 of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, as amended from time-to-time, are taxable under Entry No. 3(v)(da) of the said notification, provided the applicant does not opt for paying tax at the rate specified in Entry No. 3(ie) or 3(if). [Para 4.10]

Explanation —For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that for the purposes of this clause,—

Comments

3. The Budget 2005-06 seeks to cover construction of residential complexes having more than 12 residential units or apartments together with common areas within the service tax net. Most of the residential complexes at least in metropolitan cities comprise more than 12 units and also have some common area like passage, stairs, lift etc., besides common water supply. As such, all such units will be covered. Even the repair, alteration, renovation or restoration or similar services in relation to residential complex are also sought to be covered. It seems that any repair or anything done to upkeep the premises may be covered. The word ‘repair’ has wide ramifications and activity of even replastering to fix leakage or seepage of water or painting of walls or changing of floor tiles would be covered as the same can be construed as repair.

Whether estate developers or builders are covered

4. The Finance Minister in his speech (Para 146) has mentioned that additional services to be covered include construction of planned residential complexes, with more than 12 dwelling units, developed by builders. This has been interpreted by many that even estate developers or builders will be covered. The correct interpretation is that when builders hire a contractor, the payment made to such contractor would be subjected to service tax under this new category. When a builder constructs a residential complex himself for own use or subsequently sells it, the same will be out of the service tax net. In the case of construction services for commercial and industrial buildings, this was already clarified by the Government [F.No. B.2/8/2004 - TRU, dated September 10, 2004]. It is hoped that similar clarification will be issued in the case of construction of residential complexes also once the proposal are enacted.

Value of service

5. The service tax will not be charged on the entire amount of the construction contract awarded to the contractor. Instead, it will be levied on value addition on materials like cement, steel, fittings and fixtures, tiles etc., used to construct the building. Under the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the service providers can take credit of excise duty paid on such inputs. But in most of the cases, contractors procure the materials from the market which are not covered under the duty paying documents. Most of the builders do not keep the detailed accounts for the taxes they have paid on the purchase of materials or other inputs. Therefore, the service tax liability could go up manifold. To address this problem, it is expected that the Government will notify a new system of calculating service tax on such services. Probably, the same will be in line with the system available in case of commercial and industrial constructions which enjoy an abatement of 67 per cent in case of composite contracts where the gross amount charged includes the value of material cost. This has been provided vide Notification No. 15/2004-ST, dated September 10, 2004. This abatement is subject to further condition that no credit of input goods, capital goods and no benefit of exemption towards cost of goods have been availed.

In this connection, a reference can also be made to Notification No. 12/2003-ST, dated June 20, 2003. This notification exempts value of goods and materials supplied by the service providers if proper documentary evidence specially indicating the value of the goods and materials so supplied is maintained. This is subject to further condition that no input credit on such goods and materials has been claimed. If input credits have been claimed, then the service provider should pay an amount equal to such credit availed before supplying such goods or materials.

A blessing in disguise

6. In the Budget of 2004, when service tax on commercial construction was introduced, a doubt was raised by many about taxability in those cases where a residential complex also has partial commercial establishments. Now in all such cases, where a complex consists of more than twelve units, both the commercial as well as the residential portion will be taxable. Under which category it will fall, depends on the facts and circumstances of the individual case.

A good case for exclusion

7. Coming to the question, whether service tax on residential complexes is justified, one must keep in mind that objective of a fiscal levy is to provide greatestbenefit to the greatest number. In the humble opinion of the author, the tax should be minimum on "Roti, Kapada aur Makaan". The budget of this year has many good features and let this levy of service tax not spoil the party.

Lease of plots to NMMC for Indoor Recreation Centre

The NMMC proposes to set up the Indoor Recreation Centre which shall consist of a gymnasium, swimming pool and play courts, all of which facilities shall be accessible to the general public for a nominal fee. This can be considered to be a kind of a Public Amenity which is given to the citizens of the country and the public at large. Sr. No. 17 of the Twelfth Schedule under article 243W of the Constitution is with respect to 'Public amenities including street lighting, parking lots, bus stops and public conveniences'. An Indoor Recreation Centre can be considered as a kind of amenity which is given to the public by the local authority for recreation and the same would be similar to amenities provided by the Municipalities in their jurisdiction. Hence plots are leased by the applicant (a kind of pure services) to a Municipality, i.e., a local authority in relation to a function entrusted to such Municipality under article 243W of the Constitution and would be exempt as per Sr. No. 3 of Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017.

Lease of plots to NMMC for Slaughter House

Sr. No. 18 of the Twelfth Schedule under article 243W of the Constitution is with respect to 'Regulation of Slaughter Houses and Tanneries'. Hence plots leased by the applicant (a kind of pure services) to a Municipality, i.e., a local authority for setting up Slaughter Houses can be perceived to be in relation to a function entrusted to such Municipality under article 243W of the Constitution (Regulation of Slaughter Houses and Tanneries) and would be exempt as per Sr. No. 3 of Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017.

The jurisdiction of all Municipalities in India including PMC consists of Wards. Ward Offices are necessary for PMC to enable the execution or performance of all of its functions including those under article 243W of the Constitution. In the absence of the establishment by way of a Ward Office, PMC would find it impossible to function. The said services would be exempt as per Sr. No. 3 of Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017.

22.6 Distinction between construction service and works contract service

There is no doubt that construction contract is also a 'works contract'. However, under GST, distinction has been made between 'works contract service' and 'construction of complex'.

The distinction is that in case of works contract, a customer (recipient of supply of service) approaches the supplier of service (contractor) to undertake construction as per his requirements. In almost all the cases, the land is owned by or taken on lease by customer. The contractor enters into contract with customer and then undertakes construction with his own material. If the material is supplied by recipient himself (customer), then it is not works contract. It is simple contract for work.

In construction of complex, the builder or developer normally does not have any identified customer. Even if he has some identified customers before commencement of construction, he is undertaking construction activity on his own and not on basis of contract with customer. The land never belongs to the customer.

Valuation

Value is the gross value of taxable services.

However, any person providing taxable service of commercial or industrial construction or construction of complex can opt to pay service tax on 33% of gross amount charged. This is at the option of service provider. This relaxation is not available if only completion and finishing services are provided - Notification No. 1/2006-ST dated 1-3-2006. The partial exemption is available only if the gross amount charged includes value of goods and materials supplied or provided or used by provider of the commercial or industrial construction of service for providing such service (Explanation to Notification No. 1/2006-ST). However, value of land is not required to be added as it is neither goods nor material.

This simple method is not available in case the service provider provides only completion and finishing services (as in such cases, material content will be much less).

Your DREAM HOUSE; SOUGHT TO BE (T)AXED!

PAWAN AGARWAL*

The author has explained the scope and ambit of ‘Construction of Complex’ service, which is one of the nine new services that have been proposed to be brought to service tax levy in the Finance Bill, 2005. The author has analysed the provisions by comparing them with the provisions already in force in respect of ‘Construction Service’, and has suggested that, in the interest of the common man, the tax incidence on this service should be kept minimal.

Introduction

1. The concluding paragraph of the Hon’ble Finance Minister’s speech on Union Budget 2005-06, reads as follows:

One of India’s proudest sons, Dr. Amartya Sen, argues in his book ‘Development as freedom’ that development is a process of expanding the real freedoms that people enjoy. He says, "Growth of GNP or of individual incomes can, of course, be very important as means to expanding the freedoms enjoyed by the members of the society. But freedoms depend also on other determinants, such as social and economic arrangements (for example, facilities for education and health care) as well as political and civil rights." The UPA Government accepts this ethical dimension to the discussion of economic issues, and in this Budget, I have attempted to reflect that dimension. More or less the same idea was articulated two thousand years ago by Saint Tiruvalluvar who said:

"Pini Inmai Selvam Vilaivu Inbam Emam

Ani Enba Nattirkku Iv Iyndhu"

(Health, wealth, produce, the happiness, that is the result and security.

These five, the learned say, are the ornaments of polity)

In this backdrop, let us consider the fate of a middle-income and even an upper-middle income citizen. He has a dream to have a house of his own. He saves for a long period and then buys a house with the help of probably a housing finance institution. He pays stamp duty, registration charges, real estate agent’s commission, society formation charges, and consultant’ fees etc., besides the price paid to the builder. Now he will have to bear the brunt of service tax proposed to be levied in the budget. If a news item in Times of India is any indication, the prices of the residential houses will go up by minimum 3 per cent. The million dollar question begging an answer is whether service tax on housing complexes is justified?

The proposal

2. Before answering the above question, let us understand this new proposal. The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 had included services provided by a commercial concern in relation to construction, repairs, alteration or restoration of such buildings, civil structures or part thereof which are used, occupied or engaged for the purposes of commerce and industry. There was hardly any opposition to this proposal as this covered only commercial and industrial structure. However, the proposal contained in the Budget 2005-06 intends to cover even residential complexes. Clause (30a) of section 65 is proposed to be replaced by the following clause:

‘Construction of complex’ means—

(a)construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof; or

(b)completion and finishing services in relation to residential complex such as glazing, plastering, painting, floor and wall tiling, wall covering and wall papering, wood and metal joinery and carpentry, fencing and railing, construction of swimming pools, acoustic applications or fittings and other similar services; or

(c)repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services in relation to, residential complex.

Thus, it can be seen that the net is very wide and almost everything in relation to upkeep and repair of a residential premises or building is sought to be covered.

What is a residential complex

3. The new proposed clause (91a) defines a ‘residential complex’ to mean any complex comprising of—

‘(i)a building or buildings, having more than twelve residential units;

(ii)a common area; and

(iii)any one or more of facilities or services such as park, lift, parking space, community hall, common water supply or effluent treatment system, located within a premises and the layout of such premises is approved by an authority under any law for the time being in force, but does not include a complex which is constructed by a person directly engaging any other person for designing or planning of the layout, and the construction of such complex is intended for personal use as residence by such person.

(a)"personal use" includes permitting the complex for use as residence by another person on rent or without consideration;

Valuation

Valuation of the services would be at the transaction value. However, valuation with the related parties/ between various group companies needs to be properly dealt with and must be kept at the arm's length price to avoid unnecessary departmental intrusion.

However, one major change has been done in the valuation provisions in GST. In real estate sector, generally customer delays in making to the payment to the developers. Many times, the developer charges interest on such delayed payment. Such interest is outside the scope of tax net presently as no tax is charged on such interest whether it be VAT, Service Tax or Excise Duty. However, in GST regime, such interest will be included in the transaction value of supply and accordingly GST will be levied on such interest. Further, builder will need to bifurcate the interest on basic construction amount and amount of other services like PLC etc. as interest on basic amount will be chargeable at the rate of 12% (i.e. rate of main supply) and interest on other services at 18%.

Treatment of cancellations of bookings

In real estate sector, cancellations of bookings of flats/shops etc. is a very prevalent and common practice. Since the delivery period of a project is very high often extending to several years, many customers cancel their bookings of flats during the project.

Presently, developers can issue credit note and take benefit under Rule 6(3) of Service Tax Rules, 1994, in regard to the tax paid earlier on a cancelled booking when such booking is cancelled. Similar provisions exist in VAT laws also.

Same concept has been kept in GST regime, wherein a person can issue a credit note in case of cancellation of a service and take benefit of the tax paid earlier on such service. However, as per Section 34 of CGST Act, 2017, such credit note have to be shown/declared in the return of the month when such note is issued. However, there is a restriction which says that such credit note can be shown only up to in the return for the month of September of the following financial year in which supply is made.

Illustration

Suppose a supply was made in the month of August, 2017(F.Y. 2017-18). If a credit note is issued against this transaction, it can be shown in any return up to return of the month of September' 2018 (F.Y. 2018-19). However, if any credit note is issued after this date, it cannot be shown in return and therefore, its benefit cannot be taken.

This provision is going to pose a major hurdle for real estate sector because the construction projects usually take several years to complete. Therefore, various customers book their flats and then cancels the booking several many months/years later. However, the benefit will be available only for a selected period and would pose a very troublesome issue.

Exemption for construction industry withdrawn

Earlier, in service tax, Central Government has provided many construction service related exemption like construction of canal, dams, road, affordable housing projects etc. But, with the introduction of GST regime, government is looking to end this Exemption-Raj of service tax for many construction related services. Now, in GST, only pure labour contracts entered for house construction under Housing for All(Urban) Mission/Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY) and labour contracts used in construction of single residential unit otherwise than as a part of residential complex are kept exempt as per draft exemption list released by the GST council.

Major impact will be on affordable housing projects which are currently exempt from service tax and have not been kept in the exemption list of GST.

Flow of credits

In present regime, a Builder opting for Abatement under Notification No. 26/2012-ST is not eligible for CENVAT credit of inputs (Excise Duty). In GST regime, all the above duties/taxes (except stamp duty) will get subsumed, therefore a builder will be able to avail the input tax credit of all its procurement of goods/services. Therefore, it would reduce the tax costs substantially in the construction industry. Under GST, it is expected that seamless credit of all taxes paid on procurement of goods/ services will be allowed so that net outflow of GST liability would be minimized.

1.4 Rates of GST

The IGST and CGST Acts do not indicate GST rate structure.

As per section 9 of CGST Act, rate of CGST will be as notified by Central/State Government. The rate shall not exceed 20%. Same provision will be in SGST Act of each State.

Thus, total GST rate for intra-State supplies will not exceed 40% [20% CGST and 20% SGST].

As per section 5 of IGST Act, rate of IGST will be as notified by Central Government. The rate shall not exceed 40%.

CGST and IGST rates will be common all over India. SGST rates are also expected to be common all over India. However, since State Governments have sovereign powers to levy GST, the SGST rates may vary from State to State, though presently they are same.

UTGST Rates will be same as CGST Rates as these rates are within jurisdiction of Central Government.

The GST rates on goods are notified based on Customs Tariff Act, which is based on HSN Code. However, though Customs Tariff has eight digit code, only first four digits are used to notify GST rates. Thus, in many cases, for same four digit item, GST rates may vary depending on description of goods.

In case of services, service classification code is a 6 digit code. First two digits are always '99'.

CONSTRUCTION OF COMPLEX SERVICES

‘CONSTRUCTION OF RESIDENTIAL COMPLEX’- SUBJECTED TO SERVICE TAX

P.V. THAKAR*

With the passing of the Finance Act, 2005, certain new services are brought into the tax net vide, Notification No. 15/2005-ST, dated June 7, 2005 and the construction service relating to construction of complex also came into the tax net with effect from June 16, 2005. Some of the important definitions and their implications and the general and specific exemptions available through various notifications are analytically discussed here. Who will be liable to pay service tax under this service and what are the exemptions and options available to the service provider are also discussed.

Introduction

1. The construction activity was brought under the service tax net with effect from September 10, 2004. But it was limited to commercial construction, i.e., the construction of building primarily used for commercial purpose. However, in the recent Finance Bill, i.e., Finance Bill, 2005, the scope of the construction activity was proposed to be widened to include construction of building to be used for residential purpose. Since the said Finance Bill, 2005 has now become the Finance Act, 2005 and the new services in the said Act are brought into tax net from June 16, 2005 vide Notification No. 15/2005-ST, dated June 7, 2005, the construction service relating to construction of complex has also come into tax net from June 16, 2005. Some important definitions such as ‘construction of complex’, ‘residential complex’, ‘residential unit’, etc., in relation to this category are discussed in the succeeding paragraphs.

Scope of new levy on ‘construction of complex’

2. Clause (30a) of section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 defines the term ‘construction of complex’ as,—

"(a )construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof; or

(b )completion and finishing services in relation to residential complex such as glazing, plastering, painting, floor and wall tiling, wall covering and papering, wood and metal joinery and carpentry, fencing and railing, construction of swimming pools, acoustic applications or fittings and other similar services; or

(c )repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services in relation to, residential complex;"

This definition gives the scope of the category of service, i.e. , this definition gives the type of services (which are actually related to construction activity) which are taxable if provided in relation to construction of building which is primarily used for residential purpose.

According to the above definition, ‘construction of complex’ may be divided into three categories of services, they are :

(i)Construction of building or buildings itself which is used for residential purpose.

(ii)Allied services in relation to completion or finishing of complex such as glazing, plastering, painting, floor and wall tiling, wall covering and papering, wood and metal joinery and carpentry, fencing and railing, construction of swimming pools, acoustic applications or fittings and other similar services.

(iii)Repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of residential complex.

It, therefore, follows that not only construction activity of complex is taxable but also the allied services of construction as stated above are also taxable under this category. Even renovation, restoration and similar services in relation to the complex are also taxable. It can be concluded that the construction service itself and major services allied to it are now taxable if provided in relation to residential complex.

What is a ‘residential complex’

3. On analysing the definition given above, one can find that the term ‘residential complex’ is repeatedly used. The said term is very important since the construction service and its allied services are taxable only if provided in relation to ‘residential complex’. This term is defined in clause (91a) of section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 which is as follows :

"‘residential complex’ means any complex comprising of—

(i )a building or buildings, having more than twelve residential units;

(ii )a common area; and

(iii )any one or more of facilities or services such as park, lift, parking space, community hall, common water supply or effluent treatment system, located within a premises and the layout of such premises is approved by an authority under any law for the time being in force, but does not include a complex which is constructed by a person directly engaging any other person for designing or planning of the layout, and the construction of such complex is intended for personal use as residence by such person.

23.1-8 Redevelopment is subject to GST

Generally in re-development project, land is owned by a society, comprising members of the society with each member entitled to his share by way of an apartment. When it becomes necessary after the lapse of a certain period, society or its flat owners may engage a promoter (builder/developer) for undertaking re-construction. Society/individual apartment owners give 'No Objection Certificate' (NOC) or permission to the promoter (builder/developer), for re-construction. The promoter (builder/developer) constructs apartments with same or different carpet area for original owners of apartment and additionally may also be involved in one or more of the following: (i) construct some additional apartments for sale to others (ii) arrange for rental accommodation or rent payments for society members/original owners for stay during the period of re-construction (iii) pay an additional amount to the original owners of flats in the society.

Under this model, the promoter (builder/developer) receives consideration for the construction service provided by him, from two categories of service receivers. First category is the society/members of the society, who transfer development rights over the land (including the permission for additional number of apartments), to the promoter (builder/developer). The second category of service receivers consist of buyers of apartments other than the society/members. Generally, they pay by cash.

In both the cases, GST is payable as in first case, the promoter receives consideration in form of TDR and in other cases, by cash.

23.1-1 Statutory provisions in respect of construction of complex

Following is 'supply of service' as per para 5(b) of Schedule II of CGST Act.

Construction of a complex, building, civil structure or a part thereof, including a complex or building intended for sale to a buyer, wholly or partly, except where the entire consideration has been received after issuance of completion certificate, where required, by the competent authority or after its first occupation, whichever is earlier.

Explanation.- For the purposes of this clause- (1) the expression "competent authority" means the Government or any authority authorized to issue completion certificate under any law for the time being in force and in case of non-requirement of such certificate from such authority, from any of the following, namely - (i) an architect registered with the Council of Architecture constituted under the Architects Act, 1972; or (ii) a chartered engineer registered with the Institution of Engineers (India); or (iii) a licensed surveyor of the respective local body of the city or town or village or development or planning authority.

4.1 Only residential complexes having 12 or more residential units used for commercial or industrial purposes covered - From the above provision, it is evident that only the residential complexes comprising of twelve or more residential units would be covered under the scope of construction services for the purpose of service tax.

4.2 Common area and facilities with approved plan - Such a residential complex must have a common area and certain facilities, such as park, lift, parking space, etc. so that the complex can be conveniently used by the occupants. Moreover, the layout of such a premises must be approved by the competent authority. Such a complex would not include a complex which is meant for personal use of the owner. In other words, such complexes are used for commercial or industrial purposes and not for personal purposes.

4.3 Provision relating to ‘residential complex’ to be read with the provision of ‘commercial or industrial construction service’ - In this connection, it is pertinent to point out that the expression ‘residential complex’ is to be read with the provision of the taxable service of construction which has been re-defined by clause (zzq) of sub-section (105) of section 65 to read as ‘commercial or industrial construction service’. It has been explained in the below mentioned paragraph 5.

Taxable service of construction

5. Clause (zzq) of sub-section (105) of section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 originally inserted by Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 explained the meaning of the taxable service of construction as a service provided ‘to any person, by a commercial concern, in relation to construction service’. However, Finance Act, 2005 has amended this meaning to read as a service provided ‘to any person, by a commercial concern, in relation to commercial or industrial construction service.’ The expression ‘commercial or industrial construction service’ has been explained in paragraph 6 infra.

5.1 Definition of ‘construction service’ has been made more specific - The original definition of ‘construction service’ as introduced by Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 was general in nature. However, Finance Act, 2005 has made it more specific to cover commercial and industrial construction services only, thus excluding the services for personal use.

5.2 Revised definition of ‘construction services’ is inclusive and not exhaustive - Thus, from the meaning of the taxable construction service as given above, it is quite evident that the residential complex, which is the subject-matter of service tax, should be used only for commercial or industrial use. In other words, the residential complexes which are not intended for commercial or industrial use or are intended for personal use would not be subjected to service tax. Moreover, the meaning of ‘construction services’ as expanded by Finance Act, 2005 to read as ‘commercial or industrial construction service’ is wide enough and is inclusive in nature and not exhaustive. Besides the construction of residential complexes, certain other construction services, which have been pointed out in paragraph No. 22 infra, are also to be read with the expanded definition of construction services so that they are covered under ‘commercial or industrial construction services’ to attract service tax.

5.3 Services not specifically mentioned may also be subjected to service tax due to the revised definition of ‘construction services’ - Not only those services which have been specifically mentioned in paragraph No. 22 infra, other services which may be treated as commercial or industrial construction service would also attract service tax as per the revised definition of construction services; since the definition is inclusive and not exhaustive.

Meaning of Commercial or Industrial Construction Service

6. With effect from June 16, 2005, the Finance Act, 2005 has expanded the scope of construction services and the service has been renamed as ‘commercial or industrial construction service’. Thus, sub-section (25b) of section 65 of Finance Act, 1994 defines the expression ‘commercial or industrial construction service’. As per this provision, ‘commercial or industrial construction service’ means-

( a)construction of a new building or a civil structure or a part thereof; or

( b)construction of pipeline or conduit; or

( d)repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services in relation to, building or civil structure, pipeline or conduit,

23.3 GST Rate w.e.f. 1-4-2019 on various types of real estate projects

GST Rates have been specified on various types of real estate projects. These are explained below.

23.3-1 Construction of affordable residential apartments

In respect of construction of affordable residential apartments, the GST rate is CGST 0.5% plus SGST/UTGST 0.5% (total 1%) or IGST 1% (without ITC), where supply of services involves transfer of land or undivided share of land - Sr No. 3(i) and 3(ic) of Notification No. 11/2017-CT (Rate) and 8/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017 as amended w.e.f. 1-4-2019.

The GST rate will be CGST 0.75% plus SGST/UTGST 0.75% (total 1.50%) or IGST 1.50% where supply of services does not involve transfer of land or undivided share of land.

GST is payable at 1% in respect of service of construction of affordable residential apartments and at 5% in respect of construction of apartments other than affordable when project involves both categories, where price includes value of land - Crescent Builders., In re [2022] 145 taxmann.com 392 (AAR - Kerala).

This rate applies to Construction of affordable residential apartments by a promoter in (a) a Residential Real Estate Project (termed as RREP) Sr No. 3(i) and (b) Real Estate Project (termed as REP) other than RREP Sr No. 3(ic).

This rate applies to RREP or REP commenced on or after 1-4-2019. This rate also applies to an ongoing RREP or REP in respect of which the promoter has not exercised option to pay central tax on construction of apartments at full rate (after availing ITC) as specified in item 3(ie) or 3(if) of Notification No. 11/2017-CT (Rate) and 8/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017 as amended w.e.f. 1-4-2019.

In case of ongoing projects, this rate applies even in case of projects which were not coming under definition of affordable houses under earlier scheme - FAQ (Part II) No. 20 issued by CBI&C vide circular F No. 354/32/2019-TRU dated 14-5-2019.

No GST is payable where the entire consideration has been received after issuance of completion certificate, where required, by the competent authority or after its first occupation, whichever is earlier.

The contention of the applicant is that the activity is sale of land and it is neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services as per Schedule III of the CGST Act. As per Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II of the CGST Act construction of a complex, building, civil structure or a part thereof, including a complex or building intended for sale to a buyer, wholly or partly, except where the entire consideration has been received after issuance of completion certificate, where required by the competent authority or after its first occupation, whichever is earlier shall be treated as a supply of services. In the instant case, it is stated by the applicant that it is not receiving any advance from its customers for undertaking development activities in the plot and the plot is sold after development. Hence the transaction is in respect of sale of developed plots/land and is covered by Paragraph 5 of Schedule III of the CGST Act which stipulates that sale of land and, subject to clause (b) of paragraph 5 of Schedule II, sale of building shall be treated neither as a supply of goods nor a supply of service. Therefore, the transaction is not liable to GST. [Para 12]

2. Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) dated 28th June, 2017 exempts various services. In fact very first entry of the said notification exempts services provided by an entity registered under Section 12AA of the Income Tax Act, 1961 by way of charitable activities and words 'charitable activities' are defined to include advancement of religion, spirituality or yoga. Thus, charitable services provided by such trust are out of GST.

However, services received by a trust are not covered under the above entry and a person providing services to such trust has to pay GST. Construction of a building is a service and construction of temple building is also subject to GST and no exemption from GST is granted for construction of religious place like a Temple, Church, Gurudwara, Mosque etc.

Further, if construction contract is a composite contract, effective rate would be 12% provided value of land is also included in the contract value. Generally, land is not included in the price paid to the contractor who is awarded contract for construction of a temple and hence rate of 12% will not be applicable in such case. Hence, practically, construction of any religious place attracts 18% GST.

8. Section 7 CGST defines supply in an inclusive manner meaning it is a widened and broadened connotation. Essentially, a flat under construction and intended to be sold to a buyer is sale of immovable property, but when it is undergoing construction there is an element of service and consequently, it was necessary to treat construction of flats as a supply of service vide Section 7(1)(d) read with item no 5(b) of Schedule II. 9. Schedule of Goods and Service Tax rates for services approved by GST Council laying down fitment of rates of services states at entry 19 that "Construction of a complex, civil structure or part thereof intended for sale to a buyer wholly or partly" will bear GST at 12.5% with full input tax credit, but no refund of overflow of input tax credit. The entry also explains that the value of land is included in the amount charged from the service recipient. Simultaneously, rate of GST for composite works contract as defined in Section 2(119) vide entry 27 is 18% with full input tax credit. In substance and effect, though construction of flat is treated as a service yet it is akin to a works contract. Drawing such a cue implies that concession of 6% is given to factor in value of land thereby leading to a calculation of 33% of abatement on the total consideration. However, prescription of such a standard rate of abatement [assumed] does not take into realities of cheap, medium, semi-luxury, luxurious and elite segments where composition of land value would considerably vary. Moreover, in semi-rural developing towns, presumed rate of 33% in respect of land value may be on higher side leading to excess input credit over 12% output tax inasmuch as input supplies for builders mostly carry a rate of 18% to 28% which as per schedule of rates as seen above is not refundable. In cases, where input tax credit falls short of GST rate of 12% profits of builders will truncate or lead passing of burden on to consumers. In my opinion, this matters ought to have been formulated by the legislature in a flexible manner through a methodology by way of rules to reckon local factors.

10. Another daunting controversy that may arise is whether the overflow of input tax credit is to be worked per project or on a net basis for all projects put together. Section 16 of CGST provides that every person shall subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed and in the manner specified in Section 49 be entitled to the credit of any input tax in respect of any supply of goods and services or both to him which are used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of his business and the amount shall be credited to the electronic ledger of such person. In my opinion, looking at the wording of Section 16 aforesaid read with Section 17 better view appears to be that an overall picture of all projects will have to be undertaken and not project wise. No guidance is found either in the Act or the relevant rules as what are the implications of GST in a case when a project undertaken by the builder where he has to give flats to the owner of land in discharge of consideration for obtaining development rights. Assuming in a particular case, the developers have to provide 100 flats to owners and there other 200 flats for free sale; in former case he will be a contractor levying GST at 18% with input tax credit, whereas in the latter case, the rate would be 12% with full input tax credit but no refund of overflow credit in a situation where flats are sold before they are fully developed. In the aforementioned example, there can controversy as to how the overflow of input tax credit to be computed being the difference between the rate of GST on input supplies and 18% GST rate more particularly, after considering common input supplies and capital goods employed for both types of flats. Moreover, disputes will arise as to what is time of supply of the 100 units to be allotted to owners more specifically, if land is not parted physically at one go, but in stages. Can we say the supply of flats is complete when possession of land is given despite the fact that flats are yet to be constructed? If the free sale flats are sold in stages question will emanate as to whether input tax credit is to be accumulated or can be claimed while construction is progressing without any sale? It would be best to issue clarifications on these and other potential roadblocks that may lead to avoidable litigation.

Amended provision relating to construction services 3. The Finance Act, 2005 has substituted the aforesaid original provision relating to construction services with the following provision as contained in the revised clause (30a) of section 65 of Finance Act, 1994-

"‘construction of complex’ means-

( a)construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof; or

( b)completion and finishing services in relation to residential complex such as glazing, plastering, painting, floor and wall tiling, wall covering and wall papering, wood and metal joinery and carpentry, fencing and railing, construction of swimming pools, acoustic applications or fittings and other similar services; or

( c)repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services in relation to, residential complex."

3.1 New provision relating to residential complexes - Thus, the expression ‘construction service’ as contained originally in sub-section (30a) of section 65 has been substituted by ‘construction of complex’, meaning thereby that the provision has been made more specific and is restricted to the construction of residential complexes having twelve or more residential units. This is a new provision introduced by Finance Act, 2005. As a result, the construction of a single residential unit would not be covered for the purpose of service tax.

3.2 New nomenclature for construction services - To explain the revised meaning of the expression ‘construction service’, as originally provided by Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004, Finance Act, 2005 inserted new clause (25b) in section 65, with the nomenclature of ‘commercial or industrial construction service’. The expanded meaning has been explained in paragraph 5 infra.

3.3 Exemption of construction of complexes - Notification No. 18 of 2005, dated June 7, 2005 exempts taxable service of construction of complex from service tax, as is in excess of service tax calculated on 33 per cent of the gross amount charged from any person by any such service provider for providing taxable service. In other words, the effective rate of tax on construction of residential complex shall be 3.36 per cent of the gross amount charged from any person by the service provider. This exemption shall not apply if the taxable services provided are only completion and finishing services in relation to the residential complex.

3.4 When exemption is not applicable - The exemption will not apply if the service provider has taken Cenvat Credit of duty paid on inputs or capital goods or Cenvat credit in respect of service tax paid on input services. So, the service provider has two options - either to pay service tax at the rate of 3.36 per cent and to forego the Central credit. Alternatively, he may avail Cenvat Credit and pay full tax at the rate of 10.2 per cent. Of course, he will be able to set off tax payable against the Cenvat credit under this option.

3.5 Scope of construction services extended - Thus, the scope of construction services liable to service tax has been extended by the Finance Act, 2005 by bringing the following construction services, which were so far outside the scope of service tax, within the service tax net:

( i)Renovation services of commercial and industrial complexes;

( ii)Construction of conduits or pipelines and repairs, alteration, renovation or similar services in relation to conduits or pipelines;

( iii)Construction of residential complexes;

( iv)Completion and finishing services in relation to commercial and industrial complexes and residential complexes.

These new services will attract service tax from June 16, 2005.

It will sell plots of land inside the complex to prospective buyers who will enter into a works contract with the applicant for the construction of residential units. The applicant itself will execute a part of the works contract [‘activity No. 3’] and for remaining part, the applicant will further enter into a works contract with other contractors [‘activity No. 4’]. However, goods for construction will be purchased/acquired by the applicant and the property in those goods will be transferred to buyers of the housing units and such transfer would be exigible to tax as sale of goods. The applicant sought advance ruling of the Authority on questions of its liability in these two types of activities, and also on question of rate of tax in case of activity No. 3.

The applicant contends that since the works contract in activities 3 and 4 involves construction of a new building-such an activity can only be covered under(ii)( b) in the Explanation to section 65(105)(zzzza). Since the new building proposed to be constructed in the course of the execution of the works contract is a residential one, and is not for the purpose of commerce or industry, such a works contract will not fall under (b) and therefore, will not attract service tax. The applicant further states that a works contract for construction of a new building for residential purposes is also not covered under any of the remaining classifications in (ii) of the Explanation to clause (zzzza). The classification (c) which covers ‘construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof’ is not applicable in applicant’s case as the works contract is for construction of an individual residential unit and not for construction of a residential complex.

Decision in the case of Harekrishna Developers (supra )

3.3 Authority for Advance Ruling held:

1. To attract service tax under sub-clause (zzzza) of section 65(105), a works contract has to meet the two conditions: (i) and (ii) in the Explanation to sub-clause (zzzza). The facts narrated by the applicant indicated that condition (i) is met in the instant case as the transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the works contract is exigible to tax as sale of goods under the local Sales Tax Act. To meet condition (ii), the activity involved in the works contract in activity Nos. 3 and 4 has to be covered by at least one of the classifications (a ) to (e) in the Explanation to sub-clause (zzzza). Proceeding serially, one finds that building of a residential house on a sub-plot in a residential complex is clearly not covered in (a). As pointed out by the applicant itself, it is also not covered by (b) which covers construction of a new building intended primarily for commerce and industry and does not cover construction of a new building. Item (c) of sub-clause (zzzza) of clause (105) covers ‘construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof’.

2. As per the draft of the works contract submitted, it is clear that such contracts will be for construction of individual houses on sub-plots located within the plot owned by the applicant on which the applicant proposes to develop a residential housing project. As per the applicant’s own narration, the residential project to be constructed on this plot would have at least 12 residential units, a club house and other common facilities and the layout of the project would be approved by the prescribed authority under the relevant law in force. Such a project constructed as per activity Nos. 3 and 4 squarely conforms to the definition of a ‘residential complex’ given in clause (91a) of section 65, and the individual houses constructed get covered under the definition of a ‘residential unit’ contained therein. Execution of the works contract, thus, involves construction of a part of a new ‘residential complex’ and is covered by (c).

Thus, service tax exemption is not available to pure service activities such as real estate, architecture, legal or interior decoration services, etc., even if the works contract services of the principal contractor are exempt.

Conclusion

8.The concept of outsourcing all activities, barring the core area of specialization is gradually evolving globally, including in India. To avoid litigation surrounding levy of applicable tax, it is of paramount importance to have clarity on as to when does the process qualify as 'manufacture'? There are even greater complexities regarding the process involving both supply of goods and rendition of service, as identifying the correct base for levy of service tax on the service element becomes a challenging task. The proposed Goods and Services Tax ('GST') scenario looks optimistic for the job work sector when all the taxes, i.e., excise duty, service tax and VAT will get subsumed under the 'grand tax', as we may call it, and there will be one base for levy of GST without any distinction between goods and services.

30a) ‘Construction of complex’ means construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof, or completion or finishing services in relation to residential complex such as glazing, plastering, painting, floor and wall tiling, wall covering and wall papering, wood and metal joinery and carpentry, fencing and railing, construction of swimming pools, acoustic applications or fitting and other similar services, or repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services in relation to, residential complex . This is a very long and complex definition having not less than 75 words. Hence, one has to understand the definition of construction of complex by breaking it in several parts. Let us try to understand the above definition in detail :-

1.The complex must be a residential complex.

2.In case of construction service, naturally, it must be a new residential complex.

3.In case of completion and finishing services, which is also defined as construction of complex, the complex must be residential complex but there is no need to see that it is a new residential complex.

4.The definition of construction of complex also includes repair, alteration, renovation or similar services to the new as well as existing residential complexes.

Now we one has to go for definition of the Residential complex and this definition is given in section 65(91a).

Residential Complex - Meaning of

3. As per section 65(91a) ‘Residential complex’ means any complex means comprising of-

( i)a building or buildings, having more than twelve residential units;

( ii)a common area; and

( iii)any one or more of facilities or services such as park, lift, parking space, community hall, common water supply or effluent treatment system, located within a premises and the lay out of such premises is approved by an authority under any law for the time being in force, but does not include a complex which is constructed by a person directly engaging any other person for designing or planning of the layout and construction of such complex is intended for personal use as residence by such person.

Not all the residential complexes come under the definition of complex for the purpose of taxability of this service but it must have at least 13 residential units along with some common area and common facilities. Hence one should note the clear fact that construction of residential complex having up to 12 residential units is out of the preview of the service tax.

The common facilities mentioned here are illustrative only and the complex may have any other type of common facility or facilities but interestingly the Circular No. F.No.B1/6/2005-TRU, dated July 27, 2005 has mentioned market or shopping complex, schools, security, banks, gymnasium, health club, sports facilities, power back up and the like. Some of the constituents of the illustrative list given in the above circular are irrelevant in context to the residential complex but his shows the provision of taxation on this service is so complex and tough to understand.

Further a very strange condition is also attached with this definition of residential complex and this condition is that the lay out of the complex must be approved by an authority under any law for time being in force. Hence the unauthorized construction will be out of the net of service tax. Though it seems to be strange but this is the law as mentioned above and also showing the quality of taxation in our country.

Residential complex for personal use

4. As per section 65(91a)( iii) if the residential complex is constructed for personal use of the service receiver than it will be out of the definition of residential complex and no service tax is payable. For this purpose an Explanation is added to section 65(91a), which is being reproduced here :-

Explanation.-For removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that for the purpose of this clause-

( a)‘Personal use’ includes permitting the complex for use as residence by another person on rent or without consideration.

( b)‘Residential unit’ means a single house or a single apartment intended for use as a place of residence.

If a person is constructing a residential complex for his own purpose or for the purpose of giving it on rent to any other person by retaining the ownership of the same by not selling it and at the time of construction he takes the services of other person for planning and lay out then the same will not be taxable to service tax. The tax is applicable only when a builder builds a residential complex for sale to other person or persons and in the process if he uses the services of other person for construction.

5. What is exactly taxable - A checklist

The whole taxability has been made so complex by jugglery of definitions that it is very difficult to understand the same without summarizing the whole contents. Here is an attempt to summarise it all for better understanding :-

1.Service tax is applicable when a builder, deve-loper or promoter constructs a residential complex having at least 13 residential units for sale to other person or persons and uses the services of any other person for construction.

2.If a person builds a residential complex for himself and not for sale by using the services of any other person for construction, no service tax is payable.

3.Service tax is not payable for residential complexes having 12 residential units or less.

The Floor Area Ratio (FAR), also known as the Floor Space Ratio (FSR) or the Floor Space Index (FSI), depicts the relationship between the total usable floor space in a building and the total area of the plot on which the building is constructed. In mathematical terms, FAR = CA/LA, where CA = Constructed area or built-up area, and LA = Land area. [Para 4.8] According to the Project Plan submitted at the time of the hearing, FAR for the entire project is 2.749 after deducting from the total built-up area the common areas like lift-lobby, stair area etc. FAR for the affordable residential apartments in the project should, therefore, be atleast 1.375. The total plot size being 5627 sq. mtr., the built-up area for affordable residential apartments should atleast be 7734 sq. mtr. The built-up area for the affordable residential apartments, as identified by the architect, under the RREP is 7885 sq. mtr. (the calculation sheet is attached). The relevant FAR, therefore, comes out to be 1.401, which is 50.96 per cent of the FAR for the project. The RREP, therefore, is an affordable housing project in terms of the AHP Notification. FINANCE BILL, 2006 (AS PASSED BY LOK SABHA)

Service Tax on Construction Industry

Service tax on ‘construction industry’ comes under fire in this article. After having imposed service tax on industrial and commercial construction a few years back, the Finance Minister has stretched the levy to residential construction also. The author in a very lucid way has explained the types of construction services and tax imposable on them. The changes introduced in the Finance Bill, 2006 have also been cited. All these changes will be effective from date of enactment of the Finance Bill, 2006.

RAJKUMAR S. ADUKIA*

Introduction

1. The exponential growth of the ‘construction industry’ has surely not gone unnoticed. At least, the Government has an eye on the sector. The biggest award that the Government gives to all growing sectors is taxes - asking for their share in the growth. Also the Government has been smart enough to levy the same in a phased manner so that it goes smoothly without attracting too much burden. After imposing service tax on industrial and commercial construction under the entry ‘construction of industrial or commercial buildings’ few years back, the Finance Minister had stretched the levy to ‘residential constructions’ also. So much for the National Policy of providing a shelter to all and consequent concessions to the industry being given under Direct Tax Laws, the sub-section targets the construction activity for the not so privileged, namely, residential complexes. Nevertheless, the levies have been imposed and it will be better to discuss them rather than complaining.

Construction of complex service

2. This is one of the latest services to be included in the service tax basket. It has been added through a sub-clause (zzzh) of clause (105) of section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 that reads as:

"(105) ‘taxable service’ means any service provided or to be provided,—

( zzzh)to any person, by any other person, in relation to construction of complex,

and the term ‘service provider’ shall be construed accordingly."

The levy has been made under a new sub-clause and has not been made by amending the sub-clause (zzzq) of clause (105) of section 65 dealing with commercial or industrial construction service. Though currently all services are being charged at a common rate of 10 per cent plus a surcharge amounting to 2 per cent, (12 per cent once the Finance Bill gets approved) this may, however, mean that in the long run the Finance Minister may have plans to tax commercial construction and residential construction at different rates.

The charging clause is clear and covers all service providers and all persons receiving the service. Unlike some other services where the service is taxable only if provided to a client or customer, in the case of commercial complex, the service is taxable when it is offered to any other person. This means that even sub-contractors providing services to a contractor or builder will have to collect and deposit service tax and will have to make all the compliances. The main contractor can take CENVAT credit for the same.

2.1 What is construction of a complex? - The term has been defined in clause (30a) of section 65 as—

"30(a) ‘construction of complex’ means—

(a )construction of new residential complex or a part thereof; or

(b )completion and furnishing services in relation to residential complex such as glazing, plastering, painting, floor and wall tiling, wall covering and wall papering, wood and metal joinery and carpentry, fencing and railing, construction of swimming pools, acoustic applications or fittings and other similar services; or

(c)repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services in relation to, residential complex."

In all the above 3 sub-clauses (a), (b) and (c ), there is a common phrase which also needs proper definition for clear understanding.

2.2 What is a residential complex?

"(91a) ‘residential complex’ means any complex comprising of—

(i )a building or buildings, having more than twelve residential units;

(ii )a common area; and

(iii )any one or more of facilities or services such as park, lift, parking space, community hall, common water supply or effluent treatment system,

located within a premises and the layout of such premises is approved by an authority under any law for the time being in force, but does not include a complex which is constructed by a person directly engaging any other person for designing or planning of the layout, and the construction of such complex is intended for personal use as residence by such person."

The intra-State supply and inter-State of services by way of grant of license or lease to explore or mine petroleum crude or natural gas or both is exempt from so much of the CGST or IGST as is leviable on the consideration paid to the Central Government in the form of Central Government's share of profit petroleum as defined in the contract entered into by the Central Government in this behalf - Notification No. 5/2017-CT (Rate) and No. 5/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 25-1-2018.

Since the exemption is to the extent of Centre's share of profits, it is possible that State Governments may not grant parallel exemption. Hence, relevant notification of State Government will have to be seen.

29.9 Real Estate Leasing and Renting Services

Renting or leasing services fall under group 99721. The GST rate is 18% (9% CGST and 9% SGST). Since place of supply is location of immovable property, IGST is not leviable.

Limited coverage of real estate services in GST - The definition of 'service' is very wide at it covers anything other than 'goods'. However, para 5 of Schedule III of CGST Act States that activity of sale of land and subject to para 5(b) of Schedule II, sale of buildings is neither supply of goods nor supply of services.

Para 5(b) of Schedule II covers sale of a flat or commercial premises in a complex.

As per Entry No. 49 of List II of Seventh Schedule to Constitution, 'taxes on lands and buildings' is a State subject.

Though Constitution grants concurrent powers to Union and State to levy GST, these are subject to recommendation of GST Council. Thus, GST on land and buildings can be imposed only to the extent recommended by GST Council.

In respect of land and buildings, the CGST Act and SGST Act makes some 'deeming provisions' in Schedule II of CGST Act.

Thus, excluding those 'deemed supply' provisions, GST cannot be imposed on other transactions relating to land and buildings.

Leasing of industrial units for 99 years of developed plots is taxable under heading 9972 - Leasing of developed industrial plots in food park for 99 years is subject to GST under heading 9972 @ 18% [9% CGST plus 9% SGST] - Greentech Mega Food Park (P.) No separate tax for supply of land or undivided share of land as part of composite supply of flats - When a builder sales flat to buyer, he also transfers to him undivided share of land by way of lease or sub-lease. The service falls under heading 9972.

In such cases, the value of service for GST is Nil, if the amount charged for such lease or sub-lease is one-third of total amount charged for composite supply or less than one-third of total amount charged - Sr. No. 16(ii) of Notification Nos. 11/2017-CT (Rate) and 8/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017 inserted w.e.f. 25-1-2018.

4. In view the observations made, the AAR ruled that the applicant was liable to pay service tax in respect of the proposed activity under sub-clause (zzzh) of section 65(105).

Conclusion 5. The findings of the AAR clearly point to the fact that services provided/to be provided in relation to ‘construction of complex’ would not only cover the ‘construction services’, but also all other services implicit in such construction. The developer provides a package of services which attract service tax. Again, the developer cannot escape the liability to service tax merely because he remains owner till the completion of the construction, for the ultimate fact is that the applicant does everything to honour its commitment to the customer from whom he receives valuable consideration in instalments. Only that construction gets excluded from the purview of residential complex and from service tax net where a complex is constructed by a person directly engaging the services of any other person for designing or planning of the layout, and after completion of construction, it is meant to be used for residential purpose either by him or his lessee or a person permitted by him. This ‘excluding clause’ cannot be applied in case of a developer merely because the ownership and possession, for the time being, vests in him. After construction is completed, the ownership and possession will be transferred to the other persons who have booked the complexes, which implies that the developer is providing services of constructing residential complexes to the other party. The present ruling of the authority amply clarifies the scope of service tax in relation to construction of complexes.
